이번 방송에서는 서울대병원 가정의학과 조비룡 교수와 함께 노화 방지 의료의 현재 수준을 알아봅니다. 실제로 효과가 입증된 생활습관과 치료는 무엇인지, 근감소증과 대사질환 관리는 왜 중요한지, 건강기능식품이나 항노화 주사·호르몬 치료는 어느 정도 근거가 있는지, 앞으로 노화 연구와 의료가 어떤 방향으로 발전할지 자세히 짚어봅니다.

나이가 들수록 체력과 회복력이 떨어져 고민되는 분, 건강수명을 늘리는 방법이 궁금한 분, 항노화 치료와 건강정보 중 무엇을 믿어야 할지 헷갈리는 분들은 실시간 채팅으로 질문 남겨주세요.

nuevos.titulo_original: Why meat eaters gained more muscle in this study #nutrition #protein
nuevos.descripcion:
Two recent clinical trials have looked at the effect of removing animal protein from the diet on muscle mass in older people.

In the first study, adults over 65 on a vegan diet for 12 weeks lost about 5% of thigh muscle volume, protein intake dropping to 0.8g/kg/day. Those on the vegan diet who also did strength training lost muscle too, just about half as much.

In the second study, adults over 55 who were doing resistance training three times a week and following mostly vegetarian diets saw an increase in muscle mass. Those who were eating some meat in their diet gained more muscle in their arms and legs and had a higher protein intake.

You can build muscle on a predominantly plant-based diet as long as your total protein intake is adequate and includes sources that provide all the essential amino acids required for muscle maintenance.

nuevos.titulo_original: Raw vs Cooked Broccoli: The Sulforaphane Difference
nuevos.descripcion:
How you prepare broccoli can change how much sulforaphane you absorb by about ten times. In lab tests on cells, sulforaphane switches on the cells' own detox enzymes.

Broccoli doesn't store sulforaphane. It stores a raw material called glucoraphanin, and young broccoli sprouts are especially rich in it. Sulforaphane forms when glucoraphanin meets an enzyme called myrosinase, which happens when you crush or chew the plant. Heat destroys myrosinase. When men ate crushed raw broccoli, about 37% of the sulforaphane reached their blood and urine. Cooked, it was 3.4%.

But even when sulforaphane gets into the blood, human trials have mostly found small effects or none.

outliers.titulo_original: ENTRAINMENT GOVERNS YOUR ENERGY & FOCUS
outliers.descripcion:
Entrainment is one of the most powerful aspects of our biology.

Our circadian rhythm is created within us, but numerous studies show that our health is best when it is entrained to the rising and setting of the sun. That’s not to say you have to wake up at sunrise, but people who try to live nocturnally definitely suffer health consequences and people who match their sleep rhythm even somewhat to the rising and setting of the sun (one form of entrainment), derive many health benefits.

Entrainment works on shorter time scales too. Exercise at roughly the same time for a few days and you’ll notice your energy will increases a few minutes before that typical workout time.

Study or do some reading or some other form of work or learning at roughly the same time or times per day, and you’ll notice that your mental sharpness will start to increase in anticipation of those times.

To be clear, some of this is psychological, but a lot of it is physiological. The neuromodulators, hormones and neurotransmitters that regulate alertness and focus are readily susceptible to entrainment.

And entrainment is a concept that we can leverage. Not to make us rigid, but understanding it can help you make better sense of why you are more energetic and mentally sharp at particular times of day, and it can give you flexibility over what those times are.

outliers.titulo_original: 414 ‒ Resistance training as we age: exercise selection, training intensity, and much more
outliers.descripcion:
In this episode, Peter welcomes back Jeff Cavaliere, a physical therapist, strength coach, and founder of ATHLEAN-X who has spent decades bridging the gap between rehabilitation, athletic performance, and strength training. Jeff begins by sharing how his experience working with professional athletes and managing his own injuries has shaped his approach to building strength and muscle while minimizing injury risk. He discusses how training should evolve as we age, particularly for those in their 40s, 50s, and beyond who want to continue making progress without compromising long-term joint health. Jeff explains why excessive training volume can be counterproductive and how to balance reps in reserve with training to failure to maximize results while managing fatigue and injury risk. He also explores the differences between training for aesthetics and functional performance, explaining why these goals are not necessarily at odds. The conversation then shifts to a muscle-by-muscle breakdown of effective exercises for building strength and hypertrophy. Jeff highlights common training mistakes, offers modifications for those dealing with pain or injury, and explains why often-neglected muscles deserve more attention.
